V.1
The quantum worldline and its cuts

We start by rigorously introducing the quantum worldline, writing a
Schwinger parametrisation for it and
canonicalising
it,
i.e. writing it in a unique representation. The idea that Schwinger parameter space is particularly apt for studying the soft expansion of this object is inspired by the derivation Steven Weinberg proposes in chapter 13 of ref.
[
81
]
for the leading-order term of the quantum worldline (
\lambda^{-n}
in the soft expansion), which he used to extract the Coulomb potential from the classical limit of symmetrised ladder diagrams. The first sub-leading correction to the quantum worldline in the soft parameter for a massless probe particle moving in the gravitational background of a massive object (e.g. bending of light) has been computed in
[
82
]
(
\lambda^{-n+1}
in the soft expansion). Here we derive all leading and sub-leading soft corrections up to
\lambda^{0}
for the scattering of two objects of arbitrary masses, show their connection with graph-theoretical constructions such as forests, and express them in a compact resummed form. This derivation and the extension presented here also share common tools with diagrammatic derivations of Time-Ordered Perturbation Theory
[
71
,
70
]
, Flow-Oriented Perturbation Theory
[
73
]
, as well as the Cross-Free Family representation and its variants
[
68
,
69
,
72
]
.
The general quantum worldline with
n
vertices
V=\{1,...,n\}
reads:

\mathscr{L}(V,\{\},p)=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{\pi}^{V}(\{q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n})\left[\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{i}{(p+\sum_{j=1}^{i}q_{\pi(j)})^{2}-m^{2}+i\varepsilon}\right]\tilde{\delta}\left(\Bigg(p+\sum_{j=1}^{n}q_{j}\Bigg)^{2}-m^{2}\right),

(94)

where
\{\}
indicates an empty set of vertices on the right side of
the cut, as we are looking at the uncut worldline, and
\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{\pi}^{V}
is the numerator associated with the quantum worldline (specifically vertices on the quantum worldline), stripped of
i
vertex factors. This expression also includes the case in which a vertex couples the matter lines to multiple massless particles, instead of one only. Indeed,
\mathscr{L}
implicitly depends on the number of cubic and quartic vertices contained in the ground set
V
. In this case, one simply has to identify the momentum
q_{j}
injecting at the
j
-th vertex with the sum of the momenta of the massless particles injecting at that vertex.

We rewrite
\mathscr{L}(V,\{\},p)
by expressing propagators in their Schwinger parametrisation

\frac{\pm i}{p^{2}-m^{2}\pm i\varepsilon}=\int\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau e^{-ip^{2}\Delta\tau}\Theta(\mp\Delta\tau).

(95)

More specifically, for the permutation
\pi
corresponding to the ordering
\pi(1)<\pi(2)<...<\pi(n)
, the propagator with momentum
q_{\pi(1)}+p
will be labelled by the proper time difference
\Delta\tau_{\pi(1)\pi(2)}
, while the propagator with momentum
q_{\pi(1)}+...+q_{\pi(j)}+p
will be labelled by the proper time difference
\Delta\tau_{\pi(j)\pi(j+1)}
. Finally, for the summand labelled by
\pi
we will use the Fourier representation for the Dirac delta function integrated over the proper time
\tau_{\pi(n)}
:

\tilde{\delta}\left(\Bigg(p+\sum_{j=1}^{n}q_{j}\Bigg)^{2}-m^{2}\right)=\int\mathrm{d}\tau_{\pi(n)}e^{-i\tau_{\pi(n)}((p+\sum_{j=1}^{n}q_{j})^{2}-m^{2})}.

(96)

In summary, we obtain:

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(V,\{\},p)=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\int\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{\pi(j)\pi(j+1)}\Theta\big(-\Delta\tau_{\pi(j)\pi(j+1)}\big)e^{-i((p+\sum_{l=1}^{j}q_{\pi(l)})^{2}-m^{2})\Delta\tau_{\pi(j)\pi(j+1)}}\right]\times

\displaystyle\times\int\mathrm{d}\tau_{\pi(n)}e^{-i\tau_{\pi(n)}((p+\sum_{j=1}^{n}q_{j})^{2}-m^{2})}\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{\pi}^{V}(\{q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}),

(97)

Let us now perform a change of variable. For the product of integrals corresponding to a fixed permutation
\pi
, we change variables to

\Delta\tau_{\pi(j)\pi(j+1)}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{i=\pi(j)}^{\pi(j+1)-1}\Delta\tau_{i,i+1}\quad&\text{if }\pi(j+1)>\pi(j)\\
\displaystyle-\sum_{i=\pi(j+1)}^{\pi(j)-1}\Delta\tau_{i,i+1}\quad&\text{if }\pi(j)>\pi(j+1)\end{cases},\quad\tau_{\pi(i)}=\tau_{n}+\sum_{j=\pi(i)}^{n-1}\Delta\tau_{j,j+1}.

(98)

When
n=2
, we saw in our warm-up example that this change of variables maps the
\Delta\tau_{12},\tau_{2}
variables of the identity permutation to themselves, while it maps the
\Delta\tau_{21},\tau_{1}
variables of the non-trivial permutation to
\Delta\tau_{21}=-\Delta\tau_{12}
,
\tau_{1}=\Delta\tau_{12}+\tau_{2}
. Under this change of variables, the integration sign and summation sign can be exchanged, giving

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(V,\{\},p)=

\displaystyle\int\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{jj+1}e^{-i((p+\sum_{l=1}^{j}q_{l})^{2}-m^{2})\Delta\tau_{jj+1}}\right]\Bigg[\mathrm{d}\tau_{n}e^{-i\tau_{n}((p+\sum_{j=1}^{n}q_{j})^{2}-m^{2})}\Bigg]\times

\displaystyle\times

\displaystyle\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\Theta\big(-\Delta\tau_{\pi(j)\pi(j+1)}\big)\right]\exp\left\{-2i\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l,l^{\prime}=1\\
l<l^{\prime}\end{subarray}}^{n}\Delta\tau_{l,l^{\prime}}(q_{l}\cdot q_{l^{\prime}})\Theta(\pi(l)-\pi(l^{\prime}))\right\}\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{\pi}^{V}(\{q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}),

(99)

where
\tau_{\pi(j)\pi(j+1)}
should now be thought of as a linear function of the integration variables, as given in eq. (
98
).
The advantage of this representation is that it
canonicalises
the sum over permutations of the attachments to the matter line.

As a simple example, for the scalar model eq. (
1
) in which numerators are trivial, eq. (
99
) coincides with eq. (
11
). Specifically, the identity permutation in eq. (
99
) contributes to the term proportional to
\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{12})
in eq. (
11
), while the other permutation, with
\pi(1)=2,\pi(2)=1
, contributes to the term proportional to
\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})
in eq. (
11
). Only the latter term is accompanied by an extra exponential
e^{-2iq_{1}\cdot q_{2}\Delta\tau_{12}}
in eq. (
11
), since such terms only arise in the presence of reversed ordering of vertices according to eq. (
99
).

For future use, let us use the notation

\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\Pi_{n}(p)

\displaystyle=\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{j,j+1}e^{-i((p+\sum_{l=1}^{j}q_{l})^{2}-m^{2})\Delta\tau_{j,j+1}}\right]\Bigg[\mathrm{d}\tau_{n}e^{-i\tau_{n}((p+\sum_{j=1}^{n}q_{j})^{2}-m^{2})}\Bigg],

(100)

\displaystyle\ell(V,\{\},p)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\Theta\big(-\Delta\tau_{\pi(j)\pi(j+1)}\big)\right]\exp\left\{-2i\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l,l^{\prime}=1\\
l<l^{\prime}\end{subarray}}^{n}\Delta\tau_{l,l^{\prime}}(q_{l}\cdot q_{l^{\prime}})\Theta(\pi(l)-\pi(l^{\prime}))\right\}\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{\pi}^{V}(\{q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}),

(101)

so that

\mathscr{L}(V,\{\},p)=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{n}(p)\ell(V,\{\},p).

(102)

The advantage of these re-definitions is that, in order to derive the cancellation of super-leading contributions, only the expansion of
\ell(V,\{\},p)
needs to be studied. In particular, the inverse quadratic propagators in the exponents of
\mathrm{d}\Pi_{n}(p)
will not need to be expanded. Once super-leading contributions cancel in the sum of
\ell(V,\{\},p)
for different permutations
\pi
, all terms induced by the expansion of the shared factor
\mathrm{d}\Pi_{n}(p)
will eventually only introduce quantum corrections, simplifying considerably the combinatorics.

For the purposes of studying the classical limit of cut diagrams in the KMOC formalism, we also have to introduce the cut version of the quantum worldline. Consider a partition of the set
\{1,...,n\}
,
S_{1}\cup S_{2}=\{1,...,n\}
, where
S_{1}
is the set of vertices on the left side of the cut, and
S_{2}
is the set of vertices on the right side of the cut. Then consider all the permutations that leave the partition invariant

\mathfrak{S}(S_{1},S_{2})=\{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\,|\,\pi(\{1,...,|S_{1}|\})=S_{1},\,\pi(\{|S_{1}|+1,...,|S_{1}|+|S_{2}|\})=S_{2}\}.

(103)

Each of these permutations also corresponds to a total ordering of
\{1,...,n\}
, and the collection
\mathfrak{S}(S_{1},S_{2})
identifies all orderings such that any element of
S_{1}
is lower than any element of
S_{2}
. The cut quantum worldline reads

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(S_{1},S_{2},p)=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}(S_{1},S_{2})}\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{\pi}^{V}(\{q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n})\left[\prod_{i=1}^{|S_{1}|-1}\frac{i}{(p+\sum_{j=1}^{i}q_{\pi(j)})^{2}-m^{2}+i\varepsilon}\right]\times

\displaystyle\times\tilde{\delta}\left(\Bigg(p+\sum_{i=1}^{|S_{1}|}q_{\pi(i)}\Bigg)^{2}-m^{2}\right)\left[\prod_{i=|S_{1}|+1}^{|S_{1}|+|S_{2}|}\frac{-i}{(p+\sum_{j=1}^{i}q_{\pi(j)})^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon}\right]\tilde{\delta}\left(\Bigg(p+\sum_{j=1}^{n}q_{j}\Bigg)^{2}-m^{2}\right)\,

(104)

where the propagators on the right side of the cut are complex-conjugated, and there is an extra Dirac delta function for the cut matter line.
In this case, the proper-time parametrisation reads

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(S_{1},S_{2},p)=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}(S_{1},S_{2})}\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{\pi}^{V}(\{q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n})\int\left[\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{\pi(j)\pi(j+1)}e^{-i((p+\sum_{l=1}^{j}q_{\pi(l)})^{2}-m^{2})\Delta\tau_{\pi(j)\pi(j+1)}}\right]

\displaystyle\times\Bigg[\mathrm{d}\tau_{\pi(n)}e^{-i\tau_{\pi(n)}((p+\sum_{j=1}^{n}q_{j})^{2}-m^{2})}\Bigg]\left[\prod_{j=1}^{|S_{1}|-1}\Theta\big(-\Delta\tau_{\pi(j)\pi(j+1)}\big)\right]\left[\prod_{j=|S_{1}|+1}^{|S_{1}|+|S_{2}|-1}\Theta\big(\Delta\tau_{\pi(j)\pi(j+1)}\big)\right].

(105)

We perform the change of variables given in eq. (
98
), exchange the sum over permutations and the integration sign. Eventually, we obtain

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}

\displaystyle(S_{1},S_{2},p)=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi(p)\ell(S_{1},S_{2};p),

(106)

with

\displaystyle\ell(S_{1},S_{2};p)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{\pi}^{V}(\{q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n})\exp\left\{-2i\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l,l^{\prime}=1\\
l<l^{\prime}\end{subarray}}^{n}\Delta\tau_{\begin{subarray}{c}l,l^{\prime}\end{subarray}}(q_{l}\cdot q_{l^{\prime}})\Theta(\pi(l)-\pi(l^{\prime}))\right\}\times

\displaystyle\times\left[\prod_{j=1}^{|S_{1}|-1}\Theta\big(-\Delta\tau_{\pi(j),\pi(j+1)}\big)\right]\left[\prod_{j=|S_{1}|+1}^{|S_{1}|+|S_{2}|-1}\Theta\big(\Delta\tau_{\pi(j),\pi(j+1)}\big)\right].

(107)

This provides the canonicalised expression for the cut quantum worldline. The integration measure of the cut contribution is completely aligned with that of the virtual contribution, analogously to the principle underlying the Local Unitarity method
[
74
,
75
]
.

V.2
Classical expansion of the quantum worldline

(a)

The forest contributing to
\mathscr{F}_{0}(V)

(b)

The forests contributing to
\mathscr{F}_{1}(V)

(c)

A selection of the forests contributing to
\mathscr{F}_{2}(V)

(d)

A selection of the forests contributing to
\mathscr{F}_{3}(V)

Figure 2
:
Examples of forests contributing to
\mathscr{F}_{k}(V)
for
|V|=4

Studying the expansion of
F_{[G]}
is equivalent to studying the expansion of
\ell(V,\{\},p)
and
\ell(S_{1},S_{2};p)
. Due to the power-counting argument, the order at which
\ell(V,\{\},p)
and
\ell(S_{1},S_{2};p)
have to be expanded upon is at most
n-1
relative to the leading order.

Triangulation identities
While a naive expansion of
\ell
features an exploding number of terms, many of them undergo significant simplifications from identities of the same type as that in eq. (
13
). Another example of such identities is

\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\Theta(\tau_{\pi(i+1)}-\tau_{\pi(i)})=1.

(108)

The identities are effectively based on the following triangulation: let
F
be a set on the ordered ground set
(1,...,n)
, that is a collection of couplets
(j,j^{\prime})
, with orientation fixed such that
j<j^{\prime}
, and with no loops.
F
corresponds to a partial ordering of the ground set
\{1,...,n\}
, or equivalently to an acyclic subgraph of the complete directed acyclic graph on the ground set
(1,...,n)
(a directed acyclic graph is actually a richer object than a partial ordering, see the notion of transitive closure). These partial orderings can be organised according to their cardinality. In fig.
2
, we provide examples of partial orderings written in terms of forests: two vertices are ordered, one being located at a higher time than another, if a directed edge departs from the first to end on the other. For example, in (a), the vertices are not ordered at all, while in (b), only two vertices have an ordering, but their ordering relative to any other vertex is not fixed. Accordingly, consider the set of all directed acyclic graphs with
l
edges that can be constructed on the
ordered
ground set
V=(1,...,n)
:

\mathscr{P}_{l}(V)=\left\{F\subset(V\times V)\,\big|\,|F|=l,\ \forall e=(v_{i},v_{j})\in F,\ i<j\right\}.

(109)

We also define the restriction of this set under the request that its elements have no loops

\mathscr{F}_{l}(V)=\left\{F\subset(V\times V)\,\big|\,F\text{ is a directed forest (arborescence)},\ |F|=l,\ \forall e=(v_{i},v_{j})\in F,\ i<j\right\}.

(110)

\mathscr{F}_{l}(V)
describes the subset of elements of
\mathscr{P}_{l}(V)
whose contribution to the observable survives the classical limit in the KMOC formalism.
Now, let
\mathfrak{S}_{n}(F)
be the set of all permutations that preserve the partial ordering implied by a specific element
F\in\mathscr{P}_{l}(V)
. If the reference ordering
(1,...,n)
gives a total ordering of vertices,
F
only gives partial ordering relations between the vertices. Then

\displaystyle\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}(F)}\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\Theta(\tau_{\pi(j)}-\tau_{\pi(j+1)})=\prod_{a=(v^{\prime},v)\in F}\Theta(\tau_{v}-\tau_{v^{\prime}}).

(111)

See refs.
[
81
,
71
,
68
,
72
,
69
]
for uses of sub-classes of this set of identities, and in particular ref.
[
72
]
for what concerns partial orderings and ref.
[
68
,
69
]
for what concerns acyclic graphs. We proceed to the expansion of
\ell(V,\{\},p)
in the scalar case, namely when
\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{\pi}^{V}=1
. We will later discuss the case of scalar QED. We consider the soft expansion

\ell(V,\{\},p)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\lambda^{m}\ell^{(m)}(V,\{\},p)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\lambda^{m}\left[\frac{\mathrm{d}^{m}}{\mathrm{d}\lambda^{m}}\ell(V,\{\},p)\bigg|_{q_{j}=\lambda\bar{q}_{j},\tau_{i}=\lambda^{-1}\bar{\tau}_{i}}\right]_{\lambda=0},

(112)

we have, of course, that

\displaystyle\ell^{(0)}(V,\{\},p)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{\pi(j),\pi(j+1)})=1.

(113)

This term, once integrated, gives the analogous of eq. (13.6.7) of ref.
[
81
]
with
quadratic propagators
instead of eikonal ones:

\displaystyle\int\mathrm{d}\Pi(p)\ell^{(0)}(V,\{\},p)

\displaystyle=\tilde{\delta}\left(\left(p+q_{1n}\right)^{2}-m^{2}\right)\prod_{j=1}^{n}\tilde{\delta}\left(\left(p+q_{1j}\right)^{2}-m^{2}\right).

(114)

In the context of this section, we only integrate back from Schwinger parameters for pedagogical reasons. As explained before, integration should really follow the step at which real and virtual contributions are combined. The first order coefficient in the expansion reads

\displaystyle\ell^{(1)}(V,\{\},p)

\displaystyle=-\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\left[\prod_{j=0}^{n}\Theta\big(-\Delta\tau_{\pi(j),\pi(j+1)}\big)\right]\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l,l^{\prime}=1\\
l<l^{\prime}\end{subarray}}^{n}2i\Delta\tau_{l,l^{\prime}}(q_{l}\cdot q_{l^{\prime}})\Theta(\pi(l)-\pi(l^{\prime}))

(115)

\displaystyle=-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l,l^{\prime}=1\\
l<l^{\prime}\end{subarray}}^{n}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{l,l^{\prime}})2i\Delta\tau_{l,l^{\prime}}(q_{l}\cdot q_{l^{\prime}}).

(116)

We see that every term in the sum corresponds to a defined ordering of
l
and
l^{\prime}
, which extends to a partial ordering of the set of
\{1,...,n\}
.

General formula
For
m<n
, we can write

\displaystyle\ell^{(m)}(V,\{\},p)

\displaystyle=\frac{(-i)^{m}}{m!}\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\left[\prod_{j=0}^{n}\Theta\big(-\Delta\tau_{\pi(j),\pi(j+1)}\big)\right]\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l,l^{\prime}=1\\
l>l^{\prime}\end{subarray}}^{n}2\Delta\tau_{l,l^{\prime}}q_{l}\cdot q_{l^{\prime}}\Theta(\pi(l)-\pi(l^{\prime}))\right)^{m}

(117)

\displaystyle=(-i)^{m}\sum_{k=0}^{m}\sum_{F\in\mathscr{P}_{k}(V)}\sum_{\vec{j}\in\{1,...,m\}^{|F|}}\delta_{j_{1}+...+j_{k},m}\prod_{e=(v,v^{\prime})\in F}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{e})\frac{1}{j_{e}!}(2\Delta\tau_{e}q_{v}\cdot q_{v^{\prime}})^{j_{e}}.

(118)

Now each term of
\mathscr{L}^{(m)}(V,\{\},p)
obtained by stripping away all the sums corresponds to a partial ordering of
\{1,...,n\}
obtained by establishing the ordering of at most
m
couplets. The sum over
k
counts the amount of distinct pairs of vertices that are ordered. A summand with index
k
will be feature a product of
k
Heaviside theta functions imposing the particular ordering. When integrating back, this means that
n-k-1
lines will be cut.

Integrating back, diagrammatics
More precisely, integrating
\ell^{(m)}(V,\{\},p)
back from Schwinger parameter space will require to choose a different integration basis of proper time differences
\{\Delta\tau_{e}\}_{e\in F^{\prime}}
for each of the summands in a forest
F\in\mathscr{F}_{k}(V)
. Such integration basis are constrained by the request that
F\subseteq F^{\prime}
, as we wish the integration variables to be aligned with the content of the Heaviside theta functions for ease of integration, which is then trivial. For
m<n
, this demand does not completely fix the change of variables, which will re-introduce a degree of arbitrariness in how the final result is written. In particular, by their very own nature, valid changes of variables can be mapped one-to-one to the potentially many spanning arborescences
F^{\prime}\in\mathscr{F}_{n}(V)
such that
F\subseteq F^{\prime}
. Integrating these terms back undoes the canonicalisation that we achieved by going to proper time space. Consider the most general integral that can appear from the expansion of the quantum worldline, namely

\displaystyle I=\int\left[\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{i,i+1}e^{-i\Delta\tau_{i,i+1}D_{i}}\right]\prod_{e\in F}\Delta\tau_{e}^{n_{e}}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{e}^{y_{e}}).

(119)

with
y_{e}\in\{0,1\}
,
n_{e}\in\mathbb{Z}
,
e\in\mathscr{K}(V)
, where
F\subset\mathscr{K}(V)
, and
\mathscr{K}(V)
is the set of edges of the complete graph on
V
. We choose a spanning arborescence
F^{\prime}
such that
F\subseteq F^{\prime}
, and write

\displaystyle I=\int\left[\prod_{e=(i,j)\in F^{\prime}}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{e}\text{exp}\left\{-i\Delta\tau_{e}\sum_{l=i}^{n-1}\sigma_{el}D_{l}\right\}(\chi^{F^{\prime}\setminus F}_{e}+\chi^{F}_{e}\Delta\tau_{e}^{n_{e}}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{e}^{y_{e}}))\right],

(120)

where
\chi^{F}_{e}
is the
e
-th component of the characteristic vector of the set
F
, and
\sigma_{el}
are the components of the matrix expressing the change of variables from the basis
\{(1,2),...,(n-1,n)\}
to the basis
F^{\prime}
. The integral is now in factorised form.

The implications of this freedom of choice are best explained diagrammatically. The forests live on the complete graph:

(121)

We may remove the explicit orientation of the edges since it is anyway uniquely induced by the ordering of the vertices. The forest
F
associated with the edges that receive a correction
\Delta\tau_{e}^{n_{e}}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{e}^{y_{e}})
can be drawn as solid black lines over the forest, say
F=\{e_{1}=(1,2),e_{2}=(1,4)\}
:

F
is not a spanning arborescence, we have the freedom to complete it to either
\{e_{1},e_{2},(3,4)\}
or
\{e_{1},e_{2},(1,3)\}
. Choosing, say

}.

(124)

The benefit of drawing diagrams as in eq. (
123
) is that they only embed the constraint imposed by
F
and they let the user choose the specific completion that they want, according to their needs (e.g.
non-planarity issues
, see also ref.
[
83
]
). See fig.
3
for an example of the use of this diagrammatic convention.

A remarkably compact expression
It also turns out that the expansion of eq. (
118
) can be rewritten in a much more compact way up to orders higher than
\lambda^{n}
. In particular, up to orders higher than
\lambda^{n}
,
the corrections resum as follows
:

\boxed{\ell(V,\{\},p)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\sum_{F\in\mathscr{P}_{k}(V)}\prod_{e=(v,v^{\prime})\in F}(e^{-2i\Delta\tau_{e}(q_{v}\cdot q_{v^{\prime}})}-1)\Theta(\Delta\tau_{e})+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{n}).}

(125)

See sect.
V.3.1
for an explicit example of this resummation procedure.

Expansion of the cut quantum worldline
We now discuss the cut quantum worldline. The result is the same apart from the product of Heaviside theta functions multiplying each term:

\displaystyle\ell^{(m)}(S_{1},S_{2},p)

\displaystyle=i^{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\sum_{F\in\mathscr{P}_{k}(V)}\sum_{\vec{j}\in\{1,...,m\}^{|F|}}\delta_{j_{1}+...+j_{k},m}\left[\prod_{e=(v,v^{\prime})\in F}\frac{1}{j_{e}!}(-2\Delta\tau_{e}q_{v}\cdot q_{v^{\prime}})^{j_{e}}\right]\times

\displaystyle\times\left[\prod_{e\in F\cap(S_{1}\times S_{1})}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{e})\right]\left[\prod_{e\in F\cap(S_{2}\times S_{2})}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{e})\right].

(126)

For algorithmic purposes, it is more convenient to use the following form, where we include additional trivial factors of
1
:

\displaystyle\ell^{(m)}(S_{1},S_{2},p)

\displaystyle=i^{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}\sum_{F\in\mathscr{P}_{k}(V)}\sum_{\vec{j}\in\{1,...,m\}^{|F|}}\delta_{j_{1}+...+j_{k},m}\left[\prod_{e=(v,v^{\prime})\in F}\frac{1}{j_{e}!}(-2\Delta\tau_{e}q_{v}\cdot q_{v^{\prime}})^{j_{e}}\right]\times

\displaystyle\times\left[\prod_{e\in F\cap(S_{1}\times S_{1})}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{e})\right]\left[\prod_{e\in F\cap(S_{2}\times S_{2})}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{e})\right]\left[\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}e\in F\cap(S_{1}\times S_{2})\end{subarray}}\big(\Theta(\Delta\tau_{e})+\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{e})\big)\right].

(127)

Equivalently, one can write the cut quantum worldline as

\boxed{\ell(S_{1},S_{2},p)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\sum_{F\in\mathscr{P}_{k}(\mathbb{Z}_{n})}\prod_{e=(v,v^{\prime})\in F}(e^{-2i\Delta\tau_{e}(q_{v}\cdot q_{v^{\prime}})}-1)(\sigma_{e}^{1}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{e})+\sigma_{e}^{2}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{e}))+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{n}),}

(128)

with

\sigma_{e}^{i}=\begin{cases}1\quad\text{if }e\notin S_{i}\times S_{i}\\
0\quad\text{otherwise}\end{cases}.

(129)

We discussed the case of a massive scalar whose interaction with the massless field is momentum independent. For a theory with non-trivial numerators associated to the massive lines, the expansion is more involved. The ordering structure of the expansion, encoded in
\mathscr{P}_{k}(V)
, remains the same, much like the Heaviside theta structure associated with a particular forest
F\in\mathscr{P}_{k}(V)
. However, the specific quantity that is associated to each expanded edge may vary.

Quantum worldline in scalar QED
Let us take the example of scalar QED. We start by splitting the set of vertices into those of valence three,
V_{3}
, that couple to one photon only and those of valence four,
V_{4}
, that couple to two photons simultaneously. In order to write the numerator, let us number these vertices according to the following convention
V_{3}=\{1,...,l\}
,
V_{4}=\{l+1,...,n\}
,
V=V_{3}\cup V_{4}
and consider a permutation
\pi
of the full vertex set:

\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{\pi}^{V}=\prod_{v\in V_{4}}-2g^{\mu_{v}^{1}\mu_{v}^{2}}\prod_{v\in V_{3}}\left(q_{v}+2\left(p+\sum_{n=1}^{\pi(v)-1}q_{\pi(n)}\right)\right)^{\mu_{v}},

(130)

where each three-point vertex
v
is associated with one photon polarisation index
\mu_{v}
, each four-point vertex
v
is associated with two photon polarisation indices
\mu_{v}^{1,2}
, and the momentum
q_{v}
is the overall momentum entering the vertex
v
coming from a single or double photon attachment. We canonicalise this numerator by choosing the same reference ordering we chose for the Schwinger parametrisation, namely
\pi=\mathds{1}
. This choice naturally leads to the rescaled numerator

\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{\pi}^{V}(\lambda)=\prod_{v\in V_{4}}-2g^{\mu_{v}^{1}\mu_{v}^{2}}\prod_{v\in V_{3}}\left(V_{v}+2\lambda\left(\sum_{n=1}^{\pi(v)-1}\bar{q}_{\pi(n)}-\sum_{j=1}^{v-1}\bar{q}_{j}\right)\right)^{\mu_{v}},\quad V_{v}=q_{v}+2\Bigg(p+\sum_{j=1}^{v-1}q_{j}\Bigg).

(131)

We have
\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{\pi}^{V}(0)=\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{\mathds{1}}^{V}
, left unexpanded. Expanding additional terms in the numerator in
\lambda
under the soft limit rescaling,
q_{k}\to\lambda\bar{q}_{k}
, on top of the scalar products appearing in the exponent of the Schwinger parameterisation, we obtain a new expansion for the quantum worldline. In order to write it compactly, let us consider, for a given forest
F
, the forest
\tilde{F}
obtained by flipping the orientation of all edges, and let
F_{u}
be the underlying undirected graph of both
F
and
\tilde{F}
. Let

\displaystyle\mathscr{T}(F)

\displaystyle=\{T\subset F\cup\tilde{F}\,|\,|\partial_{T}^{-}(v)|\leq 1,\,\forall v\in V_{3},\,|\partial_{T}^{-}(v)|=0,\,\forall v\in V_{4}\},

(132)

\displaystyle V(T)

\displaystyle=\{v\in V\,|\,|\partial_{T}^{-}(v)|=0\},

(133)

where
\partial_{T}^{-}(v)
is the set of edges that inject into
v
in the graph
T
. An element in
\mathscr{T}(F)
is associated to the part of the classical expansion due to the numerator. Then, we consider the object

W(F)=\{(F_{1},F_{2})\,|\,F_{1}\subseteq F,\ F_{2}\in\mathscr{T}(F),\ (F_{1}\cup F_{2})_{u}=F_{u}\}.

(134)

Observe that while
(F_{1}\cup F_{2})
may have multi-edges, its underlying undirected graph cannot, since multi-edges are mapped to the same edge. Then, we can write a sum over the partial orderings defined in eq. (
109
),

\displaystyle\ell(V,\{\},p)=

\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n}\sum_{F\in\mathscr{P}_{k}(V)}\left[\prod_{e=(v,v^{\prime})\in F}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{e})\right]\sum_{(F_{1},F_{2})\in W(F)}\left[\prod_{e=(v,v^{\prime})\in F_{1}}(e^{-2i\Delta\tau_{e}(q_{v}\cdot q_{v^{\prime}})}-1)\right]\times

\displaystyle\times

\displaystyle\left[\prod_{e=(v,v^{\prime})\in F_{2}}-2s_{e}^{F_{2}}q_{v}^{\mu_{v^{\prime}}}\right]\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}v\in V(F_{2})\cap V_{3}\end{subarray}}V_{v}^{\mu_{v}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}v\in V_{4}\end{subarray}}-2g^{\mu_{v}^{1}\mu_{v}^{2}}+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{n}),

(135)

where
s_{e}^{F}
is equal to minus one if the orientation of
e
has to be flipped in
F
in order to match that of the corresponding edge in
F_{1}
, and is equal to one otherwise. This formula can be easily turned into a generation algorithm for quantum worldline expressions. We can see the first forest
F_{1}
as describing the expansion terms of the exponentials, while the forest
F_{2}
describes expansion terms of the numerator. If
(v_{i},v_{j})
belongs to
F_{2}
, then
q_{i}^{\mu_{j}}
appears in the summand corresponding to
(F_{1},F_{2})
. The constraint that
|\partial_{T}^{-}(v_{i})|\leq 1
is related to the request that each Lorentz index should appear only once. Indeed, if we were to allow sets of the form
F_{2}=\{(1,2),(3,2)\}
, then they would correspond to a term of the form
q_{1}^{\mu_{2}}q_{3}^{\mu_{2}}
, which does not make sense.

For future purposes, let us also introduce the related quantity: given an arborescence
F
, rooted at any vertex (not necessarily at
v_{1}
as established by the reference ordering)

\displaystyle\ell^{F}(V,\{\},p)=

\displaystyle\left[\prod_{e=(v,v^{\prime})\in F}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{e})\right]\sum_{(F_{1},F_{2})\in W(F)}\left[\prod_{e=(v,v^{\prime})\in F_{1}}(e^{-2i\Delta\tau_{e}(q_{v}\cdot q_{v^{\prime}})}-1)\right]\times

\displaystyle\hskip 113.81102pt\times\left[\prod_{e=(v,v^{\prime})\in F_{2}}-2s_{e}^{F_{2}}q_{v}^{\mu_{v^{\prime}}}\right]\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}v\in V(F_{2})\cap V_{3}\end{subarray}}V_{v}^{\mu_{v}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}v\in V_{4}\end{subarray}}-2g^{\mu_{v}^{1}\mu_{v}^{2}},

(136)

where
s_{e}^{F_{2}}
is defined as above with reference to the new canonical ordering given by
F
.

Let us generate the quantum worldline with two attachments of single photons using this machinery. We start by generating the elements of
\mathscr{P}_{k}
, which for the ground set
\{1,2\}
give
\{\emptyset,\{(1,2)\}\}
. Define
F_{1}=\{(1,2)\}
,
F_{2}=\{(2,1)\}
and
F_{3}=\{(1,2),(2,1)\}
. We have

\displaystyle\mathscr{T}(\emptyset)=\{\emptyset\},\quad\mathscr{T}(F_{1})=\{\emptyset,F_{1},F_{2},F_{3}\},

(137)

and

\displaystyle W(\emptyset)=\{(\emptyset,\emptyset)\},\quad W(\{(1,2)\})=\{(F_{1},\emptyset),(\emptyset,F_{1}),(\emptyset,F_{2}),(\emptyset,F_{3}),(F_{1},F_{2}),(F_{1},F_{1}),(F_{1},F_{3})\}.

(138)

Finally, we have

\displaystyle V(\emptyset)=\{1,2\},\quad V(F_{1})=\{1\},\quad V(F_{2})=\{2\},\quad V(F_{3})=\{\emptyset\}.

(139)

To each element in
W(\emptyset)
and
W(\{(1,2)\})
we associate now a term in the quantum worldline with two attachments:

\displaystyle(\emptyset,\emptyset)

\displaystyle\rightarrow V^{\mu_{1}}V^{\mu_{2}}

(140)

\displaystyle(F_{1},\emptyset)

\displaystyle\rightarrow\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})(e^{-2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}}-1)V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}=-2i\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{2}),

(141)

\displaystyle(\emptyset,F_{1})

\displaystyle\rightarrow\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})(-2q_{1}^{\mu_{2}})V_{1}^{\mu_{1}},

(142)

\displaystyle(\emptyset,F_{2})

\displaystyle\rightarrow\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})(2q_{2}^{\mu_{1}})V_{2}^{\mu_{2}},

(143)

\displaystyle(\emptyset,F_{3})

\displaystyle\rightarrow\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})(-2q_{1}^{\mu_{2}})(2q_{2}^{\mu_{1}})=\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{2}),

(144)

\displaystyle(F_{1},F_{2})

\displaystyle\rightarrow-2i\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}(2q_{2}^{\mu_{1}})V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{3})=\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{2}),

(145)

\displaystyle(F_{1},F_{1})

\displaystyle\rightarrow-2i\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}(-2q_{1}^{\mu_{2}})V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{3})=\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{2}),

(146)

\displaystyle(F_{1},F_{3})

\displaystyle\rightarrow-2i\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}(-2q_{1}^{\mu_{2}})(2q_{2}^{\mu_{1}})+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{4})=\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{2}).

(147)

The last four terms give quantum contributions, and can be discarded. The first four terms map one-to-one with the terms of the quantum worldline of eq. (
21
).

In general, the compact form of the quantum worldline, obtained after expanding and applying the triangulation identities, will depend on the theory under study. However, we see no conceptual obstacle that would forbid the application of the techniques showed for the scalar theory and scalar QED to be used for other theories of interest such as gravity.

V.3
Examples

In this section, we explicitly work out the expansion of the quantum worldline for different examples, taking advantage of the systematised method presented above to go beyond the simplest cases considered in Sections
II
and
III
. In particular, the case of a quantum worldline with three attachments will be treated in both scalar theory and scalar QED. We will also discuss the issue of self-attachments.

+

+

+

=

+2(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})

+2(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})

+2(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})

+2(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})^{2}

+2(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})^{2}

+2(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})^{2}

+4(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})

+4(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})

+4(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})

+\ldots

Figure 3
:
The scalar quantum worldline with three attachments before and after the expansion of
\ell_{3}
. In accordance with the discussion of back-integration in sect.
V.2
we draw the complete graph on three vertices by using light-gray-coloured edges. In black, we overlay the edges corresponding to the chosen basis of proper times: for example, for the double cut contribution, we chose to integrate
\Delta\tau_{12}
and
\Delta\tau_{23}
, leaving out
\Delta\tau_{13}
, which corresponds to the light-gray arc connecting the first and third vertex.

V.3.1
Three attachments in scalar theory

Schwinger parametrisation
For three attachments, we need to derive the leading, sub-leading and sub-sub-leading terms in the expansion. This is entirely consistent with the fact that the three-attachment quantum worldline appears in two-loop calculations. The quantum worldline with three attachments reads

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(V,\{\},p)=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{3}}\frac{i}{[(q_{\pi(1)}+p)^{2}-m^{2}]}\frac{i}{[(q_{\pi(1)}+q_{\pi(2)}+p)^{2}-m^{2}]}\tilde{\delta}((q_{\pi(1)}+q_{\pi(2)}+q_{\pi(3)}+p)^{2}-m^{2})

\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{12}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{23}\mathrm{d}\tau_{3}e^{-i\Delta\tau_{12}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\Delta\tau_{23}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\tau_{3}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{23})

\displaystyle+\int\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{13}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{32}\mathrm{d}\tau_{2}e^{-i\Delta\tau_{13}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\Delta\tau_{32}((q_{1}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\tau_{2}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{13})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{32})

\displaystyle+\int\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{21}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{13}\mathrm{d}\tau_{3}e^{-i\Delta\tau_{21}((q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\Delta\tau_{13}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\tau_{3}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{21})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{13})

\displaystyle+\int\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{23}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{31}\mathrm{d}\tau_{1}e^{-i\Delta\tau_{23}((q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\Delta\tau_{31}((q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\tau_{1}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{23})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{31})

\displaystyle+\int\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{32}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{21}\mathrm{d}\tau_{1}e^{-i\Delta\tau_{32}((q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\Delta\tau_{21}((q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\tau_{1}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{32})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{21})

\displaystyle+\int\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{31}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{12}\mathrm{d}\tau_{2}e^{-i\Delta\tau_{31}((q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\Delta\tau_{12}((q_{1}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\tau_{2}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{31})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{12}).

(148)

The required change of variables for each of the last five integrals follows from the linear relations that express all proper times in terms of
\Delta\tau_{12}
,
\Delta\tau_{23}
and
\tau_{3}
:

\displaystyle\Delta\tau_{21}=-\Delta\tau_{12},\quad\Delta\tau_{32}=-\Delta\tau_{23},\quad\Delta\tau_{13}=\Delta\tau_{12}+\Delta\tau_{23},\quad\Delta\tau_{31}=-\Delta\tau_{12}-\Delta\tau_{23}

(149)

\displaystyle\tau_{1}=\Delta\tau_{12}+\Delta\tau_{23}+\tau_{3},\quad\tau_{2}=\Delta\tau_{23}+\tau_{3}.

(150)

Consequently, we can use
\Delta\tau_{12}
,
\Delta\tau_{23}
and
\tau_{3}
as a common integration basis for all six contributions:

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}

\displaystyle(V,\{\},p)=\int\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{12}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{23}\mathrm{d}\tau_{3}e^{-i\Delta\tau_{12}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\Delta\tau_{23}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\tau_{3}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}\times

\displaystyle\times(-\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{23})+\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{21})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{13})e^{-2iq_{1}\cdot q_{2}\Delta\tau_{12}}+\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{13})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{32})e^{-2iq_{2}\cdot q_{3}\Delta\tau_{23}}

\displaystyle+\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{23})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{31})e^{-2iq_{1}\cdot q_{2}\Delta\tau_{12}-2iq_{1}\cdot q_{3}\Delta\tau_{13}}+\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{31})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{12})e^{-2iq_{2}\cdot q_{3}\Delta\tau_{23}-2iq_{1}\cdot q_{3}\Delta\tau_{13}}

\displaystyle+\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{32})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{21})e^{-2iq_{1}\cdot q_{2}\Delta\tau_{12}-2iq_{1}\cdot q_{3}\Delta\tau_{13}-2iq_{2}\cdot q_{3}\Delta\tau_{23}}).

(151)

Expanding up to second order in the soft expansion (again, corresponding to an expansion in the rescaling
q_{i}=\lambda\bar{q}_{i}
,
\Delta\tau_{ij}=\Delta\bar{\tau}_{ij}/\lambda
) and combining theta function together according to the following identities

\displaystyle\Theta(\tau_{i}-\tau_{j})\Theta(\tau_{j}-\tau_{k})+\Theta(\tau_{i}-\tau_{k})\Theta(\tau_{k}-\tau_{j})+\Theta(\tau_{k}-\tau_{i})\Theta(\tau_{i}-\tau_{j})

\displaystyle=\Theta(\tau_{i}-\tau_{j}),

(152)

\displaystyle\Theta(\tau_{i}-\tau_{j})\Theta(\tau_{j}-\tau_{k})+\Theta(\tau_{i}-\tau_{k})\Theta(\tau_{k}-\tau_{j})

\displaystyle=\Theta(\tau_{i}-\tau_{k})\Theta(\tau_{i}-\tau_{j}),

(153)

we obtain

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}

\displaystyle(V,\{\},p)=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{3}(p)\big[1

(154)

\displaystyle+2(-i(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}+(-i(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12})^{2})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})

(155)

\displaystyle+2(-i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}+(-i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23})^{2})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{23})

(156)

\displaystyle+2(-i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}+(-i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13})^{2})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})

(157)

\displaystyle+4i^{2}(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{12}\Delta\tau_{23}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{23})

(158)

\displaystyle+4i^{2}(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}\Delta\tau_{23}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{23})

(159)

\displaystyle+4i^{2}(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{13}\Delta\tau_{12}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})\big]+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{0}),

(160)

with

\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\Pi_{3}(p)=\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{12}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{23}\mathrm{d}\tau_{3}e^{-i\Delta\tau_{12}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\Delta\tau_{23}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\tau_{3}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}

(161)

Resummation
The worldline can also be presented in resummed form. We consider the three sets of forests, organised according to cardinality:

\displaystyle\mathscr{F}_{0}(\{1,2,3\})=\{\},\quad\mathscr{F}_{1}(\{1,2,3\})=\{(1,2),(1,3),(2,3)\},

(162)

\displaystyle\mathscr{F}_{2}(\{1,2,3\})=\{\{(1,2),(2,3)\},\{(1,3),(2,3)\},\{(1,3),(1,2)\}\},

(163)

and write

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}

\displaystyle(V,\{\},p)=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{3}(p)\Bigg[\underbrace{1}_{\text{eq.}\eqref{eq:3att_forest1}}+\underbrace{\sum_{F\in\mathscr{F}_{1}(\{1,2,3\})}\prod_{e\in F}\left(e^{-2iq_{v}\cdot q_{v^{\prime}}\Delta\tau_{e}}-1\right)\Theta(\Delta\tau_{e})}_{\text{eq.}\eqref{eq:3att_forest21},\eqref{eq:3att_forest22},\eqref{eq:3att_forest23}}

\displaystyle+\underbrace{\sum_{F\in\mathscr{F}_{2}(\{1,2,3\})}\prod_{e\in F}\left(e^{-2iq_{v}\cdot q_{v^{\prime}}\Delta\tau_{e}}-1\right)\Theta(\Delta\tau_{e})}_{\text{eq.}\eqref{eq:3att_forest31},\eqref{eq:3att_forest32},\eqref{eq:3att_forest33}}\Bigg]+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{0}).

(164)

The resummed form can also be obtained directly from eq (
151
) by writing each exponential as

e^{-2i(q_{i}\cdot q_{j})\Delta\tau_{ij}}=\underbrace{(e^{-2i(q_{i}\cdot q_{j})\Delta\tau_{ij}}-1)}_{=E_{ij}}+\underbrace{1}_{=I},

(165)

expanding in
E_{ij}
and
I
and combining Heaviside theta functions according to eq. (
152
) and eq. (
153
). Finally, the term

E_{12}E_{13}E_{23}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{23})

(166)

is purely quantum and can be dropped.

Back-integration
Again, let us integrate this expression back for the purposes of highlighting the ambiguity in the choice of integration variables. Integrating the canonical expression back will require choosing integration variables for each expansion term. This choice re-introduces a level of arbitrariness. The result is expressed as follows

\ell(V,\{\},p)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\vec{n}\in\mathbb{N}^{3}\\
n_{1}+n_{2}+n_{3}\leq 2\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\vec{y}\in\{0,1\}^{3}\end{subarray}}c_{\vec{n},\vec{y}}\,\Delta\tau_{12}^{n_{1}}\Delta\tau_{23}^{n_{2}}\Delta\tau_{13}^{n_{3}}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12}^{y_{1}})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{23}^{y_{2}})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13}^{y_{3}})+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{0})

(167)

For the orders that we are interested in, namely those such that
n_{1}+n_{2}+n_{3}\leq 2
, we can impose that the integration variables that we choose for the term
n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}
contain at least the
\Delta\tau_{ij}
terms whose corresponding power
n_{i}\neq 0
. For example, for the a term
c\Delta\tau_{12}
, we can choose either the integration variables
\{\Delta\tau_{12},\Delta\tau_{23}\}
or
\{\Delta\tau_{12},\Delta\tau_{13}\}
, while for the term
c\Delta\tau_{12}\Delta\tau_{23}
we can only choose
\{\Delta\tau_{12},\Delta\tau_{23}\}
. Using this constraint, we may integrate the quantum worldline back and obtain

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(V,\{\},p)

\displaystyle=\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})\Bigg[\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})

\displaystyle+2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\frac{\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}{((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{2}}+2i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\frac{\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}{((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{2}}

\displaystyle+2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\frac{\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-(q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2})}{((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{2}}+2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})^{2}\frac{\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}{((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{3}}

\displaystyle+2i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})^{2}\frac{\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}{((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{3}}+2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})^{2}\frac{\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-(q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2})}{((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{3}}

\displaystyle+4(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\frac{i^{2}}{((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{2}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{2}}

\displaystyle+4(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\frac{i^{2}}{((q_{1}+p)^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{2}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-(q_{1}+p)^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{2}}

\displaystyle+4(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\frac{i^{2}}{((q_{1}+p)^{2}-(q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{2}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{2}}\Bigg]+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{0}).

(168)

The result is reported diagrammatically in fig.
3
. The non-unique choice of basis for back-integrating from Schwinger parameter space fixes a forest (drawn in solid black lines) over the complete graph, whose edges outside of the forest are drawn in gray. We now proceed to discussing an example with non-trivial numerators.

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
}
},

(169)

corresponding to a vertex set of the type
V=\{v_{12},v_{3}\}
. Although the worldline has three insertions, from a conceptual level the difficulty of the expansion is related to the number of vertices, which is the same as the two-insertion case treated in sect.
III.1
. eq. (
169
) equivalently reads

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(V,\{\},p)

\displaystyle=i\left[\frac{g^{\mu_{1}\mu_{2}}(q_{3}+2(q_{1}+q_{2}+p))^{\mu_{3}}}{(q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2}+i\varepsilon}+\frac{(q_{3}+p)^{\mu_{3}}g^{\mu_{1}\mu_{2}}}{(q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2}+i\varepsilon}\right]\tilde{\delta}\left((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2}\right).

(170)

The vertex numerator associated to the four-valent vertex is already in canonical form, as it is momentum independent. We only need to canonicalise the vertex numerator associated to the cubic vertex; choosing the reference ordering
\{\{1,2\},\{3\}\}
:

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(V,\{\},p)

\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{2}(p)\Big(g^{\mu_{1}\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}+(-2i\Delta\tau_{12}(q_{3}\cdot(q_{1}+q_{2}))g^{\mu_{1}\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}-2g^{\mu_{1}\mu_{2}}(q_{1}+q_{2})^{\mu_{3}})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})\Big)+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{0}),

(171)

with
V_{3}=q_{3}+2(q_{1}+q_{2}+p)
. Once integrated back, this term has exactly the same structure as eq. (
23
), the only difference being in the numerator factor for the last summand in parenthesis.

Let us discuss the expansion of the quantum worldline with three “distinct” attachments in scalar QED. Excluding the diagrams of eq. (
169
), we remain with those featuring cubic vertices only. In particular, for a vertex set
V=\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\}
:

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}

\displaystyle(V,\{\},p)=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{3}}\frac{i^{2}(q_{\pi(1)}+2p)^{\mu_{\pi(1)}}(q_{\pi(2)}+2(q_{\pi(1)}+p))^{\mu_{\pi(2)}}(q_{\pi(3)}+2(q_{\pi(1)}+q_{\pi(2)}+p))^{\mu_{\pi(3)}}}{[(q_{\pi(1)}+p)^{2}-m^{2}+i\varepsilon][(q_{\pi(1)}+q_{\pi(2)}+p)^{2}-m^{2}+i\varepsilon]}\tilde{\delta}((q_{123}+p)^{2}-m^{2})

(172)

We now Schwinger parametrise propagators and Dirac delta function, re-arrange the expression as usual, performing the appropriate change of variables and extracting a common integration measure, corresponding to the reference ordering
(1,2,3)
:

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(V,\{\},p)=\int\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{12}\mathrm{d}\Delta\tau_{23}\mathrm{d}\tau_{3}e^{-i\Delta\tau_{12}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\Delta\tau_{23}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})-i\tau_{3}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}\times

\displaystyle\times

\displaystyle(\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{23})V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{21})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{13})e^{-2iq_{1}\cdot q_{2}\Delta\tau_{12}}(V_{1}+2q_{2})^{\mu_{1}}(V_{2}-2q_{1})^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{13})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{32})e^{-2iq_{2}\cdot q_{3}\Delta\tau_{23}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}(V_{2}+2q_{3})^{\mu_{2}}(V_{3}-2q_{2})^{\mu_{3}}

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{23})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{31})e^{-2iq_{1}\cdot q_{2}\Delta\tau_{12}-2iq_{1}\cdot q_{3}\Delta\tau_{13}}(V_{1}+2q_{2}+2q_{3})^{\mu_{1}}(V_{2}-2q_{1})^{\mu_{2}}(V_{3}-2q_{1})^{\mu_{3}}

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{31})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{12})e^{-2iq_{2}\cdot q_{3}\Delta\tau_{23}-2iq_{1}\cdot q_{3}\Delta\tau_{13}}(V_{1}+2q_{3})^{\mu_{1}}(V_{2}+2q_{3})^{\mu_{2}}(V_{3}-2q_{1}-2q_{2})^{\mu_{3}}

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{32})\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{21})e^{-2iq_{1}\cdot q_{2}\Delta\tau_{12}-2iq_{1}\cdot q_{3}\Delta\tau_{13}-2iq_{2}\cdot q_{3}\Delta\tau_{23}}(V_{1}+2q_{2}+2q_{3})^{\mu_{1}}(V_{2}-2q_{1})^{\mu_{2}}(V_{3}-2q_{1}-2q_{2})^{\mu_{3}})

(173)

with
V_{1}=q_{1}+2p
,
V_{2}=q_{2}+2(q_{1}+p)
,
V_{3}=q_{3}+2(q_{1}+q_{2}+p)
. We may now expand and combine Heaviside theta functions. We obtain:

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}

\displaystyle(V,\{\},p)=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{3}(V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle[2q_{2}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}-2q_{1}^{\mu_{2}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}-4q_{2}^{\mu_{1}}q_{1}^{\mu_{2}}+2(-i\ (q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}+(-i(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12})^{2})

\displaystyle-4iq_{2}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}+4iq_{1}^{\mu_{2}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}]V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle[2q_{3}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}-2q_{2}^{\mu_{3}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}-4q_{2}^{\mu_{3}}q_{3}^{\mu_{2}}+2(-i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}+(-i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23})^{2})

\displaystyle-4iq_{3}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}+4iq_{2}^{\mu_{3}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}]V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{23})

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle[2q_{3}^{\mu_{1}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}-2q_{1}^{\mu_{3}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}-4q_{1}^{\mu_{3}}q_{3}^{\mu_{1}}+2(-i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}+(-i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13})^{2})

\displaystyle-4iq_{3}^{\mu_{1}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}+4iq_{1}^{\mu_{3}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}]V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle[4(-i)^{2}(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{12}\Delta\tau_{23}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}+4q_{1}^{\mu_{2}}q_{2}^{\mu_{3}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}-4q_{2}^{\mu_{1}}q_{2}^{\mu_{3}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}+4q_{2}^{\mu_{1}}q_{3}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}

\displaystyle+4iq_{1}^{\mu_{2}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}-4iq_{2}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}

\displaystyle+4iq_{2}^{\mu_{3}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}-4iq_{3}^{\mu_{2}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}]\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{23})

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle[4(-i)^{2}(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}\Delta\tau_{23}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}-4q_{1}^{\mu_{3}}q_{3}^{\mu_{2}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}+4q_{3}^{\mu_{1}}q_{3}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}-4q_{3}^{\mu_{1}}q_{2}^{\mu_{3}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}

\displaystyle+4iq_{1}^{\mu_{3}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}-4iq_{3}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}

\displaystyle+4iq_{2}^{\mu_{3}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}-4iq_{3}^{\mu_{2}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}]\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{23})

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle[4(-i)^{2}(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{12}\Delta\tau_{13}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}+4q_{1}^{\mu_{2}}q_{1}^{\mu_{3}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}-4q_{2}^{\mu_{1}}q_{1}^{\mu_{3}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}-4q_{1}^{\mu_{2}}q_{3}^{\mu_{1}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}

\displaystyle+4iq_{1}^{\mu_{2}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}-4iq_{2}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}

\displaystyle+4iq_{1}^{\mu_{3}}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}-4iq_{3}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}]\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13}))+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{0}).

(174)

This concludes the derivation of the quantum worldline with three attachments in scalar QED. These results are consistent with the compact form of the worldline that we have provided in eq. (
135
). Let us see that explicitly by generating the expression of eq. (
136
) for the forest
F=\{(1,2),(1,3)\}
. In this case
\tilde{F}=\{(2,1),(3,1)\}
. Then

\displaystyle\mathscr{T}(F)=\{

\displaystyle F_{1}=\{(1,2)\},F_{2}=\{(2,1)\},F_{3}=\{(1,3)\},F_{4}=\{(3,1)\},

(175)

\displaystyle F_{5}=\{(1,2),(2,1)\},F_{6}=\{(1,3),(3,1)\},F_{7}=\{(1,3),(1,2)\},F_{8}=\{(1,3),(2,1)\},F_{9}=\{(3,1),(1,2)\},

(176)

\displaystyle F_{10}=\{(1,2),(2,1),(1,3)\},F_{11}=\{(1,2),(1,3),(3,1)\}\}.

(177)

\mathscr{T}(F)
contains subsets of
F\cup\tilde{F}
that satisfy the following property: if we take such subsets, for example
\{(1,2),(2,1),(1,3)\}
, and we extract the last entry of each of the edges in it, giving
(2,1,3)
, there should not be repetition. In terms of graph orientation, this property is rephrased into the requirement that each vertex must have at most one edge injecting into it. For any element of
T\in\mathscr{T}(F)
the function
V(T)
precisely extract those vertices that have no edges injecting into them. For example
V(F_{2})=\{2,3\}
and
V(F_{6})=\{2\}
.

We are now able to construct
W(F)
, which is obtained by gluing together subforests of
F
(in the first entry below) with elements in
\mathscr{T}(F)
in such a way that covers the original forest
F

\displaystyle W(F)=\{(F_{1},F_{3}),(F_{1},F_{4}),(F_{3},F_{1}),(F_{3},F_{2}),(F_{7},\emptyset),(\emptyset,F_{7}),(\emptyset,F_{8}),(\emptyset,F_{9}),...\}.

(178)

where
...
indicates all tuples
(F^{\prime},F^{\prime\prime})
such that
|F^{\prime}|+|F^{\prime\prime}|>2
, which will give quantum terms upon application of eq. (
174
). Leaving these terms out,
W(F)
contains eight elements, exactly the number of terms that multiply
\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})
in eq. (
174
). We can use eq. (
136
) to translate one into the other. For example, for the element
(F_{7},\emptyset)
, we have
V(\emptyset)=\{1,2,3\}
and thus:

\displaystyle(F_{7},\emptyset)

\displaystyle\rightarrow\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}(e^{-2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}}-1)(e^{-2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}}-1)

(179)

\displaystyle=(2i)^{2}(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{3}).

(180)

Instead, for the element
(F_{3},F_{1})
, we have

\displaystyle(F_{3},F_{1})

\displaystyle\rightarrow\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}(-2q_{1}^{\mu_{2}})V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}(e^{-2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}}-1)

(181)

\displaystyle=4i\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})V_{1}^{\mu_{1}}q_{1}^{\mu_{2}}V_{3}^{\mu_{3}}(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{3}).

(182)

As a final example, let us consider the term
(\emptyset,F_{8})
, which gives the term

\displaystyle(\emptyset,F_{8})

\displaystyle\rightarrow\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})(-2q_{1}^{\mu_{3}})V_{2}^{\mu_{2}}(2q_{2}^{\mu_{1}}).

(183)

Figure 4
:
Cut scalar quantum worldlines corresponding to two specific choices of
S_{1}
and
S_{2}
.

We saw that the definition of the cut quantum worldline depends on a partition of the set of vertices. The partitions of
\{1,2,3\}
are

\displaystyle S_{1}^{1}=\{1\},\ S_{2}^{1}=\{2,3\},\quad S_{1}^{2}=\{2\},\ S_{2}^{2}=\{1,3\},\quad S_{1}^{3}=\{3\},\ S_{2}^{3}=\{1,2\},

\displaystyle S_{1}^{4}=\{1,2\},\ S_{2}^{4}=\{3\},\quad S_{1}^{5}=\{1,3\},\ S_{2}^{5}=\{2\},\quad S_{1}^{6}=\{2,3\},\ S_{2}^{6}=\{1\}.

(184)

Let us show how to write the cut quantum worldline for the partitions
S_{1}^{1},S_{2}^{1}
and
S_{1}^{5},S_{2}^{5}
. We have:

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(S_{1}^{1},S_{2}^{1},p)

\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{3}(p)\left(\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{23})+e^{-2i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{23})\right)

(185)

\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{3}(p)\left(1-2i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}(1-i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{23})\right)+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{0}).

(186)

In resummed form:

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(S_{1}^{1},S_{2}^{1},p)

\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{3}(p)\left(1+(e^{-2i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}}-1)\Theta(\Delta\tau_{23})\right)+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{0}).

(187)

\mathscr{L}(S_{1}^{1},S_{2}^{1},p)
is represented in fig.
4
after integration of the Schwinger parameters. It gives

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(S_{1}^{1},S_{2}^{1},p)

\displaystyle=\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})

\displaystyle+2i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\frac{\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}{((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{2}}

\displaystyle+2i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})^{2}\frac{\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})\delta((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}{((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{3}}+\ldots,

(188)

In fig.
4
we also represent
\mathscr{L}(S_{1}^{5},S_{2}^{5},p)
. In this case, after introducing Schwinger parameters, the quantum worldline reads:

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}

\displaystyle(S_{1}^{5},S_{2}^{5},p)=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{3}(p)\left(e^{-2i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{13})+e^{-2i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}-2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})\right)

\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{3}(p)\big(1-2i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}(1-i(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23})-2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}(1-i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13})\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})

\displaystyle+(-2i)^{2}(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{23}\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})\big).

(189)

After the integration of Schwinger parameters, we obtain

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(S_{1}^{5},S_{2}^{5},p)

\displaystyle=\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})

\displaystyle+2(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})\tilde{\delta}^{\prime}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})

\displaystyle+2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\frac{\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-(q_{1}+p)^{2})\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}{((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{2}}

\displaystyle+2(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})^{2}\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2})\tilde{\delta}^{\prime\prime}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-m^{2})\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})

\displaystyle+2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})^{2}\frac{\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-(q_{1}+p)^{2})\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}{((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{3}}

\displaystyle+2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})(q_{2}\cdot q_{3})\frac{\tilde{\delta}^{\prime}((q_{1}+q_{2}+p)^{2}-(q_{1}+p)^{2})\tilde{\delta}((q_{1}+q_{2}+q_{3}+p)^{2}-m^{2})}{((q_{1}+p)^{2}-m^{2}-i\varepsilon)^{2}}+\ldots.

(190)

The difference in amount of expansion terms in
\mathscr{L}(S_{1}^{1},S_{2}^{1},p)
and
\mathscr{L}(S_{1}^{5},S_{2}^{5},p)
is explained by how “close” the partitions entering the cut worldline are to the reference ordering
(1,2,3)
.

Introducing numerators does not change significantly the derivation shown here for the scalar case which, analogously to the case of the non-cut quantum worldline, has to be canonicalised.

The cut quantum worldline features terms including derivatives of Dirac delta functions. For all the examples treated in this paper, these terms will however drop in the expression of the classical impulse. Furthermore, cancellations between virtual and real contributions are manifested more easily when the expression is written in the form eq. (
127
). For
\mathscr{L}(S_{1}^{2},S_{2}^{2},p)
, for example, this prescription amounts to the following representation for its expansion:

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}

\displaystyle(S_{1}^{2},S_{2}^{2},p)=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{3}(p)\left(e^{-2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}}\big(\Theta(\Delta\tau_{13})+e^{-2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{13})\big)\right)

(191)

\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{3}(p)\big(1-2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}(1-i(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12})\underbrace{(\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{12})+\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12}))}_{=1}

\displaystyle-2i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}(1-i(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}))\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{13})

\displaystyle+(-2i)^{2}(q_{1}\cdot q_{3})\Delta\tau_{13}(q_{1}\cdot q_{2})\Delta\tau_{12}\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{13})\underbrace{(\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})+\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{12}))}_{=1}\big)+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{2}),

(192)

where we simply used the partition of the identity
1=\Theta(\Delta\tau_{12})+\Theta(-\Delta\tau_{12})
. In other words, we rewrote the expansion of the cut quantum worldline in the following form

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}

\displaystyle(S_{1},S_{2},p)=\sum_{n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}=1}^{n}\sum_{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\sigma_{3}\in\{\pm 1\}}c_{n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}}^{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\sigma_{3}}\Delta\tau_{12}^{n_{1}}\Delta\tau_{23}^{n_{2}}\Delta\tau_{13}^{n_{3}}\Theta(\sigma_{1}\Delta\tau_{12})\Theta(\sigma_{1}\Delta\tau_{23})\Theta(\sigma_{1}\Delta\tau_{13}).

(193)

This organisation of the result in a polynomial of
\Delta\tau_{ij}
and
\Theta(\pm\Delta\tau_{ij})
will lead to an algebraic realisation of super-leading cancellation, as well as of propagators raised to third power or higher and derivatives of Dirac delta functions. It will also help in manifesting the worldline form.

VI
Expansion of the KMOC integrand

The soft expansion for the integrand of an equivalence class of diagrams,
F_{[G]}
defined in eq. (
91
), can be organised in steps: first, one expresses
F_{[G]}
in terms of the quantum worldline in Schwinger space, and expands the worldlines
\ell(V,\{\},p_{i})
and
\ell(S_{1},S_{2},p_{i})
appearing in the virtual contribution and real contribution respectively. This is sufficient to realising the cancellation of super-leading contributions, up to some subtleties in the treatment of massless propagators in the radiation region. Then, one integrates such expansion using the integration measure
\mathrm{d}\Pi_{n}(p_{1})\mathrm{d}\Pi_{m}(-p_{2})
, and finally the result is re-expanded in the classical limit one last time.

At each step, we will obtain expressions that are equivalent up to higher order in the classical expansion. We divide the expansion in two distinct stages as it will be beneficial to use properties of the intermediate expansion terms to derive general considerations on the shape of the final expansion. In particular, the two-step procedure is meant to eliminate certain ambiguities that would arise by expanding diagrams such as mushroom diagrams and to reduce considerably the amount of intermediate terms.

VI.1
Zero-measured cuts

In order to both get cancellations and re-write the classical result in terms of retarded propagators, one needs to frequently invoke the vanishing of certain collections of cuts. In the context of this paper, a zero-measured cut is any collection of signed cuts (namely selecting a specific energy sign for the cut particle) that upon deletion leaves out a graph that has at most one incoming particle with positive energy or at most one outgoing particle with positive energy. In other words, they correspond to vacuum decays or decays of the particles in the theory (and their time-reversed counter-parts) which are either kinematically degenerate or kinematically forbidden. We already presented an instance of such cuts in the context of the example of sect
III
. In that instance, the kinematically forbidden process is identified by the
v_{1}
vertex, and we can schematically write:

(194)

Fig.
5
provides some more examples of processes that are kinematically forbidden: if the cut graph contains such processes, then we say it is a zero-measured cut. Indeed, in all cases, the phase-space for these processes is either empty or degenerate.

(a)

(b)

(c)

(d)

Figure 5
:
Processes that are kinematically forbidden or degenerate. Cuts of Feynman diagrams that isolate such processes are set to zero. Dashed lines correspond to massless particles and solid lines correspond to massive particles with equal mass.

These cuts are ill-defined since the surfaces identifies by these cuts, when they are non-empty, are in fact pinched. This implies that the coordinate transformation rule for the Dirac delta function does not work anymore, since the derivative of the argument of the Dirac delta function is either zero or discontinuous. Take, as an example, the following integration of a test function
g
:

I=\int\mathrm{d}^{4}k\mathrm{d}^{4}p\,\tilde{\delta}^{-}(k^{2})\tilde{\delta}^{+}((k+p)^{2}-m^{2})\tilde{\delta}^{+}(p^{2}-m^{2})g(k^{0},\vec{k};p^{0},\vec{p})

(195)

Solving two out of the three Dirac delta functions

\displaystyle I

\displaystyle=\pi^{3}\int\mathrm{d}^{3}\vec{k}\mathrm{d}^{3}\vec{p}\frac{\delta\left(\sqrt{|\vec{k}+\vec{p}|^{2}+m^{2}}+|\vec{k}|-\sqrt{|\vec{p}|^{2}+m^{2}}\right)}{|\vec{k}|\sqrt{|\vec{k}+\vec{p}|^{2}+m^{2}}\sqrt{|\vec{p}|^{2}+m^{2}}}g(-|\vec{k}|,\vec{k};|\vec{p}|,\vec{p})

(196)

\displaystyle=\pi^{3}\int\mathrm{d}^{3}\vec{k}\mathrm{d}^{3}\vec{p}\frac{1}{1+\frac{|\vec{k}|+\hat{k}\cdot\vec{p}}{\sqrt{|\vec{k}+\vec{p}|^{2}+m^{2}}}}\frac{\delta\big(|\vec{k}|\big)}{|\vec{k}|\sqrt{|\vec{k}+\vec{p}|^{2}+m^{2}}\sqrt{|\vec{p}|^{2}+m^{2}}}g(-|\vec{k}|,\vec{k};|\vec{p}|,\vec{p}).

(197)

\hat{k}=\vec{k}/|\vec{k}|
does not have a well-defined limit when
|\vec{k}|
vanishes. In other words, the surface defined by setting the argument of the Dirac delta function to zero does not allow for a well-defined normal vector field. The situation is rescued if the test function
g
or the integral measure provide enough suppression so that the integrand vanishes, but in general this may not be the case. For certain other observables, the ill behaviour of zero-measured cuts is lifted (for example, due to the offshellness granted to one of the cut particles) and give rise to subtle effects associated with long-range Coulomb like potentials (see e.g. recent work in a KMOC context in refs.
[
84
,
85
]
). A systematic incorporation of such effects into our framework is beyond the scope of the current work.

More in general, any time the argument of a Dirac delta function has ill-defined or vanishing gradient at the points where the argument itself is zero we can conclude that the Dirac delta function itself is ill-defined (as the change-of-variable rule is not allowed). The surfaces identified by setting such arguments to zero are said to be “pinched”
[
86
,
87
]
.

The reason these ill-defined cuts arise in the first place can be traced back to the (mis-)handling of
i\varepsilon
prescription that is inherent to working in the Minkowski representation. In three-dimensional representations, obtained by integrating out from the covariant representation the energy component of loop integrals
[
63
,
64
,
65
,
67
,
68
,
62
,
66
]
, Cutkosky cuts appear as denominators of the integrand, and their
i\varepsilon
-prescriptions can be handled separately: we can set the
i\varepsilon
-prescription to zero in those denominators that identify pinched singularities and leave it in the rest of the denominators. It follows that zero-measured cuts simply would never appear if we were to take discontinuities or compute imaginary parts of the three-dimensional representation. As a simple example, consider the following identities

\displaystyle\frac{1}{(|\vec{k}|+i\varepsilon)(|\vec{k}|-Q^{0}+i\varepsilon)}-\frac{1}{(|\vec{k}|-i\varepsilon)(|\vec{k}|-Q^{0}-i\varepsilon)}

\displaystyle=2\pi i\left[\frac{\delta(|\vec{k}|)}{|\vec{k}|-Q^{0}}+\frac{\delta(|\vec{k}|-Q^{0})}{|\vec{k}|}\right]

(198)

\displaystyle\frac{1}{|\vec{k}|(|\vec{k}|-Q^{0}+i\varepsilon)}-\frac{1}{|\vec{k}|(|\vec{k}|-Q^{0}-i\varepsilon)}

\displaystyle=2\pi i\frac{\delta(|\vec{k}|-Q^{0})}{|\vec{k}|}.

(199)

In the first case, a zero-measured cut
\delta(|\vec{k}|)
appears, while in the second, where we dropped the
i\varepsilon
-prescription in virtue of
|\vec{k}|=0
being a pinched singularity, it doesn’t. In general, carefully dropping the
i\varepsilon
-prescription from those denominators of the three-dimensional representation that identify pinched singularities will allow to avoid the appearance of zero-measured cuts. However, since for the scope of this paper we would like to work in four dimensions, we will simply set these contributions to zero by hand whenever they appear. This approach is somewhat different to that proposed in the appendix of ref.
[
88
]
in that the zero-measured cuts, in our prescription, can never contribute, consistently with the idea that pinched surfaces do not allow for any finite
i\varepsilon
-prescription.

VI.2
Classical expansion of the quantum integrand

We start by writing virtual contributions in terms of the quantum worldline. After symmetrisation, in accordance with the picture of eq. (
93
), we can rewrite
F_{[G]}^{V}
as:

\displaystyle F_{[G]}^{V}

\displaystyle=(-i)^{N_{G}}\mathscr{L}(V_{\text{up}},\{\},p_{1})\mathscr{L}(V_{\text{bot}},\{\},-p_{2})\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{E_{\text{m}}(V)}\prod_{e\in E_{\text{m}}(V)}\frac{1}{q_{e}^{2}+i\varepsilon}

(200)

\displaystyle=(-i)^{N_{G}}\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{|V_{\text{up}}|}(p_{1})\mathrm{d}\Pi_{|V_{\text{bot}}|}(-p_{2})\frac{\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{E_{\text{m}}(V)}\ell(V_{\text{up}},\{\},p_{1})\ell(V_{\text{bot}},\{\},-p_{2})}{\prod_{e\in E_{\text{m}}(V)}[q_{e}^{2}+i\varepsilon]}.

(201)

where
\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{E_{\text{m}}(V)}
is the numerator associated to the massless blobs (which have no quantum loops), stripped of
-i
factors for the vertices and
i
factors for the propagators. This is compensated by the
(-i)^{N_{G}}
overall factor. In order to write the cut contributions in terms of the quantum worldline, let us introduce an equivalence relation between cut diagrams. Starting from the equivalence class
[G]
, we let
[G]_{c}
be the set of all graphs in
[G]
that have a certain cut
c\in\mathscr{C}_{[G]}
(a consistent labelling based on the map
\phi_{\pi,\pi^{\prime}}
is assumed in order to identify the same cut
c
across different graphs in the same equivalence class
[G]
), where

\mathscr{C}_{[G]}=\bigcup_{G^{\prime}\in[G]}\mathscr{C}_{G^{\prime}}.

(202)

Then, for any
G\in[G]_{c}
, let
G_{L}^{c}=(V_{L}^{c},E_{L}^{c})
and
G_{R}^{c}=(V_{R}^{c},E_{R}^{c})
be the two graphs separated by the cut
c
, laying on the left and right of the cut, respectively. Let
N_{G_{R}^{c}}
and
N_{G_{L}^{c}}
be the number of connected massless components that are strictly on the right and left of the Cutkosky cut respectively (strictly as in: they are not cut through by the Cutkosky cut itself). Then, we can write the real integrand
F_{[G]}^{R}
in Schwinger-parameter space as

\displaystyle F_{[G]}^{R}=(-i)^{N_{G}}\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{|V_{\text{up}}|}(p_{1})\mathrm{d}\Pi_{|V_{\text{bot}}|}(-p_{2})\bar{\mathscr{N}}_{E_{\text{m}}(V)}\sum_{c\in\mathscr{C}_{[G]}}(-1)^{N_{G_{R}^{c}}}\ell(V_{L}^{c}\cap V_{\text{up}},V_{R}^{c}\cap V_{\text{up}},p_{1})\times

\displaystyle\times\ell(V_{L}^{c}\cap V_{\text{bot}},V_{R}^{c}\cap V_{\text{bot}},-p_{2})\prod_{e\in E_{\text{m}}(V)\cap E_{L}^{c}}\frac{1}{q_{e}^{2}+i\varepsilon}\prod_{e\in E_{\text{m}}(V)\cap E_{R}^{c}}\left[\frac{1}{q_{e}^{2}+i\varepsilon}+i\tilde{\delta}^{+}(q_{e})+i\tilde{\delta}^{-}(q_{e})\right]\prod_{e\in c}\tilde{\delta}^{+}(\sigma_{e}(V_{L}^{c})q_{e}),

(203)

with

\sigma_{e}(V^{\prime})=\begin{cases}1\quad&\text{if }e=(v,v^{\prime}),v\in V^{\prime},\,v^{\prime}\in V\setminus V^{\prime}\\
-1\quad&\text{if }e=(v,v^{\prime}),v\in V\setminus V^{\prime},\,v^{\prime}\in V^{\prime},\end{cases}

(204)

Observe that the integration measure for real and virtual contributions is exactly the same. In fact, we could promote the virtual contribution to a real one by simply adding to
\mathscr{C}_{[G]}
the cut crossing the two final-state massive particles. In particular, we may write

\displaystyle F_{[G]}=F_{[G]}^{V}+F_{[G]}^{R}=\int\mathrm{d}\Pi_{|V_{\text{up}}|}(p_{1})\mathrm{d}\Pi_{|V_{\text{bot}}|}(-p_{2})f_{[G]}.

(205)

We may proceed to discussing the classical expansion of the quantum worldline and the associated classical expansion of the quantum observable.
The classical expansion of
\ell
induces an expansion of the integrand
f_{[G]}
. Defining
D_{\tau}^{G}=D_{\text{soft}}^{G}-4(L+1)+|V_{\text{up}}|+|V_{\text{bot}}|
, which is obtained by subtracting the scaling of the loop integration measure and proper-time integration measure to the overall contribution of the graph to the observable, we have

\displaystyle f_{[G]}

\displaystyle=\sum_{m=0}^{N_{G}-1}\lambda^{D_{\tau}^{G}+m}f_{[G]}^{(m)}+\mathscr{O}(\lambda^{D_{\tau}^{G}+N_{G}}).

(206)

(a)

Graph representative of the equivalence class
[G]
.

(b)

Complete graph
G_{\text{comp}}
associated to the equivalence class
[G]
.

(c)

Example of element in
\mathscr{F}_{v}(G_{\text{comp}})
, where
v
is highlighted in red.

(d)

Example of element in
\mathscr{F}_{v}(G_{\text{comp}})
, where
v
is highlighted in red.

Figure 6
:
An equivalence class
[G]
(as usual, equivalence under permutation of vertices on the upper or lower massive line) defines a unique graph
G_{\text{comp}}
. A choice of a vertex
v
further defines a set of spanning arborescences
\mathscr{F}_{v}(G_{\text{comp}})
rooted at
v
whose constraint is that they contain all massless (dashed) edges. In the language of WQFT, at the red vertex one has the observable insertion, which we will later simply denote by a half-edge, following the convention from the existing literature.

Cancellation of super-leading contributions
The statement of integrand-level cancellation of super-leading contributions is summarised by the request that
f_{[G]}^{(m)}=0
for
0\leq m<N_{G}-1
. In fact, as mentioned, if we think of
f_{[G]}^{(m)}
as a multivariate polynomial in the expansion parameters of the worldline and the Feynman propagators and Dirac delta functions associated with massless propagators

f_{[G]}^{(m)}=P^{(m)}(\{\Delta\tau_{e}\}_{e\in\mathscr{K}(V_{\text{up}})},\{\Delta\tau_{e}^{\prime}\}_{e\in\mathscr{K}(V_{\text{bot}})},\{G_{F}(q_{e})\}_{e\in E_{\text{m}(V)}},\{\tilde{\delta}^{\pm}(q_{e})\}_{e\in E_{\text{m}(V)}},\{q_{e}\}_{e\in E_{\text{m}}(V)},p_{1},p_{2}),

(207)

with coefficients given by sums and differences of products of Heaviside theta functions, then requiring cancellation of super-leading contributions implies that either
(a)
the coefficients of this polynomial are all zero or
(b)
the non-vanishing terms integrate back to a zero-measured cut. These two conditions can be checked algorithmically. Let us stress that if we use the form of the quantum worldline given in eq. (
118
) and eq. (
127
), the vanishing of the coefficients (implication (a)) is algebraic,
meaning that no additional theta identity needs to be used
. For what concerns implication (b), it should also be checked without need of simplifying the result using further identities. In other words, once eq. (
118
) and eq. (
127
) have been used to write down
P^{(m)}_{[G]}
, one only needs to collect the non-zero terms contributing to it and check that they integrate back to zero-measured cuts.

Worldline form
The second fact that we would like to check is the extent to which our integrand reproduces that which can be derived using the worldline formalisms. Take
f_{[G]}^{(N_{G}-1)}
and, again, eliminate all terms that integrate to zero measured cuts. Taking
V_{\text{up}}=\{v_{1},...,v_{n}\}
and
V_{\text{bot}}=\{w_{1},...,w_{m}\}
, let
G_{\text{comp}}=(V,E_{\text{comp}})
be the graph with the same set of vertices
V
as that of the graph
G
and the edge set

E_{\text{comp}}=\mathscr{K}(V_{\text{up}})\cup\mathscr{K}(V_{\text{bot}})\cup E_{\text{m}}(V),

(208)

recalling that
\mathscr{K}(V^{\prime})
is the set of edges of the complete graph on the ground set
V^{\prime}
. For any fixed vertex on the upper line,
v\in V_{\text{up}}
, we define the following set

\mathscr{F}_{v}(G_{\text{comp}})=\{T\,|\,T\text{ is a spanning arborescence in }G_{\text{comp}}\text{ rooted at the sink }v,\ T\cap E_{\text{m}}(V)=E_{\text{m}}(V)\}.

(209)

Then, we hypothesise that, up to pieces that integrate to purely imaginary quantities, one has

\displaystyle f_{[G]}^{(N_{G}-1)}

\displaystyle=(-i)^{N_{G}}\sum_{v\in V_{\text{up}}}\left(\sum_{e\in E_{\text{m}}(v)}q_{e}^{\mu}\right)\sum_{T\in\mathscr{F}_{v}(G_{\text{comp}})}\ell^{T\cap\mathscr{K}(V_{\text{up}})}(V_{\text{up}},\{\},p)\,\ell^{T\cap\mathscr{K}(V_{\text{bot}})}(V_{\text{bot}},\{\},p)\prod_{e\in E_{\text{m}}(V)}G_{R}(s_{e}^{T}q_{e}).

(210)

where
\ell^{F}
was defined in eq. (
136
). In words, the polynomial can be written as a sum of terms, each corresponding to a specific vertex on the upper line,
v
, where the impulse is measured. For each
v
the integrand is a sum of spanning arborescences on the graph
G_{\text{comp}}
with an orientation defined by the choice of the vertex
v
. In particular, for fixed spanning arborescence
T
and vertex
v^{\prime}
, there is a unique directed path from
v^{\prime}
to
v
.

Applications and examples

VII.1
Classical limit for diagrams with one connected massless component

+

q_{1}

q_{3}

q_{6}

+

q_{1}

+

q_{1}

\approx

q_{1}
q_{2}
q_{3}
q_{4}
q_{5}

=0

Figure 7
:
An example of sum of cut diagrams that gives a classical contribution containing a zero-measured cut, which directly vanishes.

For diagrams with one connected massless component, the classical limit coincides with the leading term in the soft expansion. As we saw, for theories with a non-renormalisable self-interaction between massless particles only, power-counting alone allows to conclude that the connected massless component must be a tree diagram.

Example
Let us start with an example. Consider the sum of graphs in the equivalence class with the following representative:

q_{1}
q_{2}
q_{3}
q_{4}
q_{5}
q_{6}

(211)

with all the diagrams obtained by permuting vertices on its upper or lower massive line. The original diagram is then identified with the couplet of identity permutations
\pi=\mathds{1}
,
\pi^{\prime}=\mathds{1}
. A loop momentum basis of this graph is given, for example, by
q_{1},...,q_{5}
, and the classical limit corresponds to taking their soft limit. The leading term in the classical expansion of
F_{G}
, excluding all the zero measured cuts (namely all those in which any of the massless propagators attaching to the massive lines are cut, since all massive propagators are cut), reads

\displaystyle F_{G}=\frac{1}{3!}\mathscr{N}

\displaystyle\tilde{\delta}(2q_{1}\cdot p_{1})\tilde{\delta}(2q_{3}\cdot p_{1})\tilde{\delta}(2q_{5}\cdot p_{1})\tilde{\delta}(2q_{2}\cdot p_{2})\tilde{\delta}(2q_{4}\cdot p_{2})\tilde{\delta}(2q_{6}\cdot p_{2})\times

\displaystyle\times

\displaystyle\Bigg[q_{1}^{\mu}G_{F}(q_{1})G_{F}(q_{2})\tilde{\delta}^{+}(q_{12})G_{F}(q_{3})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{1234})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{4})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{5})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{6})^{\star}

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle(q_{1}+q_{3})^{\mu}G_{F}(q_{1})G_{F}(q_{2})G_{F}(q_{12})G_{F}(q_{3})G_{F}(q_{4})\tilde{\delta}^{+}(q_{1234})G_{F}(q_{5})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{6})^{\star}

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle iq_{3}^{\mu}G_{F}(q_{3})G_{F}(q_{4})\tilde{\delta}^{-}(q_{12})\tilde{\delta}^{+}(q_{1234})G_{F}(q_{1})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{2})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{5})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{6})^{\star}

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle q_{5}^{\mu}G_{F}(q_{5})G_{F}(q_{6})\tilde{\delta}^{-}(q_{1234})G_{F}(q_{12})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{1})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{2})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{3})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{4})^{\star}

\displaystyle-i

\displaystyle(q_{1}+q_{5})^{\mu}G_{F}(q_{5})G_{F}(q_{6})G_{F}(q_{1})G_{F}(q_{2})\tilde{\delta}^{-}(q_{1234})\tilde{\delta}^{+}(q_{12})G_{F}(q_{3})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{4})^{\star}

\displaystyle+

\displaystyle(q_{3}+q_{5})^{\mu}G_{F}(q_{5})G_{F}(q_{6})G_{F}(q_{3})G_{F}(q_{4})G_{F}(q_{1234})\tilde{\delta}^{-}(q_{12})G_{F}(q_{1})^{\star}G_{F}(q_{2})^{\star}

\displaystyle-i

\displaystyle(q_{1}+q_{3}+q_{5})^{\mu}G_{F}(q_{1})G_{F}(q_{2})G_{F}(q_{12})G_{F}(q_{3})G_{F}(q_{1234})G_{F}(q_{4})G_{F}(q_{5})G_{F}(q_{6})\Bigg],

(212)

with
G_{F}(q_{e})=(q_{e}^{2}+i\varepsilon)^{-1}
.
\mathscr{N}
is the numerator factor including all of the contribution from the massless as well as massive propagators. It factorises all contributions in the leading classical expansion since any canonicalisation step requires
\mathscr{N}_{\pi}=\mathscr{N}_{\mathds{1}}
at leading order in the classical expansion.

F_{G}
that give terms proportional to
